title: Treatment of immune checkpoint inhibitor–induced arthritis in patients with malignant melanoma using anti–interleukin-17 antibodies
summary:
Immune checkpoint inhibitors are important drugs used to treat malignant melanoma (black skin cancer), as they help the immune system fight the tumor more effectively. However, they can also cause side effects in which the immune system attacks healthy tissues. One such side effect is inflammatory joint disease (arthritis), which can lead to pain and reduced mobility.
There is evidence that the inflammatory messenger IL-17 plays an important role in this type of arthritis. Drugs that block IL-17 may help to reduce these symptoms. However, it is still unclear whether this treatment affects the effectiveness of cancer therapy.
In this study, patient data will be analyzed retrospectively to investigate how well IL-17-blocking drugs control arthritis and whether they have an impact on the course of the cancer. Both tumor outcomes and arthritis activity will be evaluated.

interventions.name: Retrospective analysis of all patients who received anti-IL-17 antibody therapy for immune checkpoint inhibitor–induced arthritis between November 2022 and November 2025.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients with ICI-induced arthritis who were treated with anti–IL-17 antibodies while receiving immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy.
Exclusion criteria:
No confirmed diagnosis of ICI-induced arthritis or no treatment with an anti-IL-17 antibody
